Reframed with insights from the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS):
- SLOOS for Q3 2020 indicates broad-based tightening of lending standards and weaker loan demand across key categories—C&I loans (to firms of all sizes), commercial real estate, consumer credit (credit cards and autos), and many residential mortgage segments. Banks cited elevated uncertainty, lower risk tolerance, and concerns about borrowers’ collateral and cash flows, particularly in CRE and pandemic-sensitive sectors.
- These credit-supply headwinds mean that, even with near-zero policy rates, ongoing Treasury and agency MBS purchases, and improved market functioning, transmission to the real economy via bank lending remained constrained—especially for small and medium-sized businesses and non-prime households.
- While policy backstops and forbearance helped sustain credit availability and mitigate near-term delinquencies, SLOOS responses suggest standards were likely to stay tight in the near term, implying a slower pass-through of accommodative policy to employment, investment, and inflation.

Net tone: cautious—strong policy support and accommodative market conditions are offset by restrictive bank lending standards and soft loan demand, which pose a meaningful drag on the recovery and downside risk to inflation.
